supremeCourt.name: Corte Suprema de Justicia de la Nación
supremeCourt.appointmentMethod: Nominated by the President, confirmed by 2/3 of the Senate.
supremeCourt.fspEraChanges: In 1990 President Menem (Peronist, pre-Kirchner) expanded the court from 5 to 9 (Law 23.774), creating an "automatic majority". In 2006 the Kirchnerist government reduced it back to 5 (Law 26.183) and had tightened the appointment process (Decree 222/03, 2003). So the packing predates the Kirchnerist (FSP-affiliated) governments, which actually de-packed it — a useful counter to a simplistic 'FSP packs courts' reading.
supremeCourt.stillServing: After the retirements of Highton (2021) and Maqueda (2024), the court fell below its 5-seat complement to 3 justices; President Milei's attempts to fill the seats by decree (Lijo, García-Mansilla) failed in the Senate (2025), leaving a deadlock as of 2026.

courtHistory.event: Earlier history: the Corte Suprema was installed in 1863 (5 justices). In 1947 Perón's Congress removed 4 of the 5 justices; the court was expanded 5→7 (1958) and returned to 5 (1966); the 1976–83 junta replaced it. Reshaping the court by incoming governments was a long-running pattern before 1990.
Law 23.774 (Menem) expanded the court from 5 to 9, creating the 'automatic majority'.
Decree 222/03 (Néstor Kirchner) opened Supreme Court nominations to public scrutiny, applied to the post-Menem vacancies.
Law 26.183 (promoted by Cristina Fernández de Kirchner) reduced the court from 9 back to 5, reversing Menem's expansion.

After Highton (2021) and Maqueda (2024) left, the court fell to 3 justices; Milei's decree appointments (Lijo, García-Mansilla) were rejected by the Senate in 2025, leaving the seats vacant amid a deadlock.

benchControl.note: Menem's 1990 expansion to 9 seats and its 'automatic majority' predate any FSP-linked government; no Kirchner-era appointees sat on the court.
Néstor Kirchner's renewal under the open Decree 222/03 process seated Zaffaroni (2003), then Highton and Lorenzetti (2004), as Menem-era justices resigned or were impeached — 1 to 3 of the 9 seats.

Four of the seven sitting justices (Zaffaroni, Highton, Lorenzetti, and Argibay from Feb 2005) were Kirchner appointees — a majority of the sitting bench, while Law 26.183 (2006) shrank the statutory size from 9 toward 5 by attrition. The ICJ described the openly-vetted renewal as strengthening independence, and the court repeatedly ruled against the government — notably striking down the 2013 judicial-council reform.

After the 2014–15 departures of Petracchi, Argibay, Zaffaroni and Fayt, Kirchner-era appointees fell to 2 of 5 (Lorenzetti, Highton) beside Macri's 2016 appointees (Rosatti, Rosenkrantz); with Highton's exit (2021) and Maqueda's (2024), 1 of the 3 sitting justices (Lorenzetti) as the Senate rejected Milei's 2025 nominees.

current: Frente para la Victoria / Frente de Todos (Kirchnerist Peronism)
fspParties.note: The Partido Justicialista (Peronism) is listed as an FSP member, together with Kirchnerist vehicles (Frente para la Victoria, Frente de Todos) and allied groups (Frente Grande, Partido Intransigente). Important caveat: Peronism is a broad movement spanning left to right, and this dossier treats only its Kirchnerist wing as FSP-aligned (following the FSP membership roster cited below), which is why the 1990s Menem and 2002–03 Duhalde (both PJ) presidencies are marked non-FSP while the Kirchners and Alberto Fernández are marked FSP. A precise seat-by-party table is deferred: Argentina renews only half its Chamber and a third of its Senate every two years, so any single chamber mixes two elections' winners and 'per-election' seat tables are easily misread.

legislativeControl.seats: Peronism governed under Menem in the 1990s and the Duhalde interim, but that PJ leadership was not the FSP-aligned Kirchnerist current; treated here as outside the FSP bloc.
The Kirchners' Frente para la Victoria held the presidency and, for most of this period, working majorities in both chambers — with a mid-term dip after the 2009 elections.
Under Macri's Cambiemos government the Kirchnerist bloc was the largest opposition force but out of power.
Alberto Fernández's Frente de Todos was the largest bloc in the Chamber of Deputies (~119 of 257) but short of a 129-seat majority; it did hold a Senate majority (~41 of 72) over this period.
The 2021 midterms cost the Frente de Todos its Senate majority — the first time Peronism lost Senate control since the 1983 return to democracy — and left it short of a majority in the Chamber too.
Under the libertarian Milei government the Kirchnerist bloc (now Unión por la Patria) is the largest opposition force but out of power.
